principle.name: Measure First, Optimize Second
principle.description: Always establish performance baselines before making optimizations. Measure current performance, identify bottlenecks, then optimize based on data-driven decisions rather than assumptions.
principle.rationale: Performance optimizations without baseline measurements are often premature and can lead to wasted effort or even performance degradation.

example.good: Measure query execution times, add indexes, then measure improvement
example.bad: Add indexes based on theoretical analysis without measuring actual impact

principle.name: Focus on High-Impact Optimizations
principle.description: Prioritize optimizations that deliver the highest performance impact for the lowest cost. Use the 80/20 rule - focus on 20% of optimizations that deliver 80% of performance gains.
principle.rationale: Not all optimizations have equal value. Concentrating on high-impact changes ensures maximum ROI on performance improvement efforts.

example.scenario: When faced with multiple performance issues
example.good: Optimize the slowest database queries first (20% effort, 80% impact)
example.bad: Make minor optimizations across many areas (80% effort, 20% impact)

principle.name: Performance Budgets and Thresholds
principle.description: Establish clear performance budgets and SLA thresholds. Every optimization should be evaluated against these predefined limits to prevent scope creep and ensure consistent user experience.
principle.rationale: Performance budgets provide objective criteria for when optimizations are "good enough" and prevent endless optimization cycles.

example.good: API responses < 200ms, database queries < 100ms, page load < 2s
example.bad: No clear performance targets leading to subjective optimization decisions

principle.name: Incremental Deployment and Testing
principle.description: Deploy optimizations incrementally with thorough testing at each stage. Use A/B testing, canary deployments, and gradual rollouts to validate improvements and minimize risk.
principle.rationale: Large-scale performance changes can have unintended consequences. Incremental deployment allows for early detection of issues and quick rollback if needed.

example.good: Implement cache for 10% of traffic, measure results, then gradually increase
example.bad: Deploy cache changes to 100% of traffic without validation

principle.name: Monitor Real-World Performance
principle.description: Ensure performance testing and monitoring reflect real-world usage patterns. Test with realistic data volumes, user behaviors, and network conditions that match production environment.
principle.rationale: Laboratory performance tests often don't reveal issues that appear in production due to different usage patterns, data distributions, and network conditions.

example.good: Use production-like data volumes and realistic user behavior patterns in tests
example.bad: Test with artificial data that doesn't match production usage patterns

principle.name: Consider System-Wide Impact
principle.description: Evaluate optimizations in the context of the entire system stack. Performance improvements in one area may create bottlenecks in another. Consider end-to-end user experience rather than isolated component performance.
principle.rationale: Optimizing one component to be extremely fast doesn't help if other components become the bottleneck. System performance is determined by the slowest component.

example.good: Analyze how database optimizations affect overall response times and system load
example.bad: Optimize database queries in isolation without considering application-level impact

convention.rule: Document optimization decisions with before/after metrics

examples.good: // Before optimization: Average response time: 450ms // After optimization: Average response time: 180ms (60% improvement)
examples.bad: // Optimized database query // Added index without measuring impact

examples.good: baseline_test, stress_test, spike_test, soak_test with documented parameters
examples.bad: Random performance tests without clear objectives

convention.rule: Consistent cache key patterns and TTL

examples.bad: Inconsistent cache keys and arbitrary TTL values

pitfall.why_problematic: Optimizing code without proper profiling and baseline measurements often leads to wasted effort and can even degrade performance.
pitfall.correct_approach: Always measure first, then optimize based on data. Establish clear performance baselines before making changes.

pitfall.why_problematic: Focusing on tiny optimizations while ignoring major architectural bottlenecks provides minimal overall performance improvement.
pitfall.correct_approach: Use profiling tools to identify the biggest performance bottlenecks first. Focus on high-impact optimizations that provide maximum ROI.

pitfall.why_problematic: Performance optimizations that work in idealized test environments often fail in production due to different data volumes, network conditions, and user behaviors.
pitfall.correct_approach: Test with realistic data volumes and usage patterns. Consider network latency, concurrent users, and data distribution in production environment.

pitfall.why_problematic: Deploying performance changes without proper monitoring makes it impossible to detect regressions or measure actual impact.
pitfall.correct_approach: Implement comprehensive monitoring before, during, and after optimizations. Set up alerts for performance regressions and establish clear SLA monitoring.

pitfall.why_problematic: Implementing caching without proper invalidation strategies leads to stale data and user experience issues.
pitfall.correct_approach: Design comprehensive cache invalidation strategies. Consider time-based, event-driven, and manual invalidation approaches. Document cache invalidation rules clearly.
